sections.title: cs.CL · Computation and Language
sections.name: Computation and Language
sections.focus: conversational AI, dialogue systems, LLM agents and retrieval-augmented generation
sections.lede: Recent research addresses core challenges in conversational artificial intelligence, examining long-horizon memory mechanisms, automated retrieval-augmented generation development, small language models for fast dialogue systems, and safety risks in economic environments. These studies provide empirical evaluations of autonomous agent capabilities and memory limitations across diverse operational contexts.

papers.title: Forget Freely, Grep Later: Lossless, Index-Free Memory for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
papers.abstract: Long-horizon LLM agents often exceed their context windows, forcing them to discard information that may be needed later. Existing context management strategies rely on summarization, masking, or structured memory, requiring decisions about what to preserve or how to retrieve it before future needs are known. However, these methods can introduce lossy compression, potentially discarding details needed for future tasks. To address this limitation, we introduce GrepMem, a simple, lossless, and index-free memory mechanism built on two components: an append-only plain-text log of the agent's complete history and a regular-expression search tool for on-demand recall. Unlike structured memory systems, GrepMem requires no embeddings, retrieval index, memory extraction, or additional models. We train Qwen3.5-9B with reinforcement learning under five context management strategies and evaluate on multi-question research sessions, long-stream recall, and agent-trajectory question answering. GrepMem achieves 95-97% accuracy on ContextBench, versus at most 21% for lossy baselines, and outperforms SUPO's summarization by 8.8 percentage points on BCP-Multi. GrepMem scales effectively to increasingly long input streams while remaining on the accuracy-token-cost Pareto frontier across all five evaluation tasks. Our results show that a plain-text log and grep provide a simple but competitive approach to long-horizon agent memory, without requiring complex structured memory infrastructure.
papers.summary: The authors introduce GrepMem, a lossless and index-free memory mechanism combining a plain-text log with regular-expression search, which achieves 95-97 percent accuracy on ContextBench and outperforms lossy baselines without requiring complex structured memory infrastructure.

papers.title: Can an LLM dream? Testing the overfitted brain hypothesis on an agent with text memory
papers.abstract: Hoel (2021) proposed that dreams distort replayed experience so that the brain does not overfit to recent events. We test this hypothesis on an LLM agent (Claude Opus 5.5) that stores what it learns in a text memory and rewrites that memory each night from the day's conversation transcript. The agent goes through ten simulated days of conversation built from LongMemEval. We corrupt 5, 10, 20 or 40 percent of the transcript's turns before each nightly rewrite in one of two ways. Detail corruption changes one or two details in a turn to plausible wrong ones, or replaces the turn with one by the same speaker from an earlier day. Random-text corruption replaces half of the selected turns with a passage of Moby-Dick and inserts Moby-Dick words into the other half. A size limit on the memory, rising from 19,500 to 117,000 tokens over ten nights, set from human free-recall data, forces it to forget. We learned that corruption did not help the agent apply what it learned in earlier conversations to new tasks in any of 30 runs (ten conditions, three different conversation histories). Replacing details in 40 percent of turns lowered recall from 76 to 60 percent. Random text had no consistent effect on recall, with a paired difference of 0 $\pm$ 2 points at 40 percent, because the model recognized it as corrupted and left it out of memory. Replaced details were stored as fact even when another turn held the correct value, and the agent answered 40 percent of those questions correctly, compared with 75 percent without corruption. These results suggest that a pretrained model can separate corrupted text from real events, so a fair test needs a learner that cannot make this separation as easily, such as a model fine-tuned on the corrupted days or an agent whose days take place in an invented world.
papers.summary: Researchers tested the overfitted brain hypothesis on a Large Language Model agent with text memory, finding that transcript corruption did not improve transfer learning and that replaced details were erroneously stored as facts.

papers.title: AutoRAGBench: A Benchmark for LLM Agents Automating RAG System Development
papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is a well-established paradigm for augmenting large language models (LLMs) with information retrieved from external corpora. However, developing effective RAG systems requires substantial engineering effort and iterative experimentation, as effective design choices vary across tasks and domains. With rapid advances in LLM agent capabilities, we ask how well these agents can autonomously build RAG systems and how effectively they can improve them through iteration. In this paper, we propose AutoRAGBench, the first benchmark to evaluate how well LLM agents develop RAG systems from scratch in an open code space. It comprises nine RAG system development tasks. For each task, agents build RAG systems from scratch without starter code or prescribed strategies, under a six-hour budget on a single H800 GPU. They analyze task data, implement RAG pipelines, and iteratively refine their designs based on experimental feedback. We evaluate nine agent configurations and analyze both the effectiveness of the resulting RAG systems and their development trajectories. GPT-6.1 Sol with Codex CLI achieves the highest average score of 56.1. The composite Human-SOTA baseline averages 44.4. These results show that LLM agents can automate effective RAG system development. When starting from a human-designed system on each of seven tasks, GPT-6.1 Sol with Codex CLI improves the score by 16.6 points on average.
papers.summary: The authors propose AutoRAGBench, a new benchmark for evaluating autonomous retrieval-augmented generation system development, finding that GPT-6.1 Sol with Codex CLI achieves the highest average score and successfully improves upon human-designed systems.

papers.title: Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB: An Open and Efficient Small Language Model for Fast Conversational Agents
papers.abstract: We introduce Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB, an open and efficient small language model further post-trained from Gemma-4-E4B-it and optimized for speed and intelligence per GB of memory used for fast conversational agents. The model carries forward Gemma's strong conversational capabilities and further improves multi-turn tool use, instruction following, and input grounding for fast, local voice/device assistants, interactive personas, and embedded/Edge interfaces. The model combines natural conversation with multi-turn agentic capabilities to power voice/device assistants, interactive characters and robotic/IoT interfaces running on GeForce RTX, Jetson, and RTX/DGX Spark. Experiments on 21 benchmarks show that Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB achieves the highest average accuracy while generating the fewest output tokens in both reasoning and non-reasoning modes, compared with Gemma-4-E4B-it and Qwen3.5-4B. The model is released with a DFlash drafter. With DFlash, Bolt E4B achieves $2.74\times$ the per-user decode speed of inference without speculative decoding at concurrency~1, and $1.21\times$ the generation throughput of Gemma-4-E4B-it with MTP at batch size 1.
papers.summary: We introduce Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB, an open and efficient small language model further post-trained from Gemma-4-E4B-it and optimized for speed and intelligence per GB of memory used for fast conversational agents.

papers.title: When Helpful Agents Cause Financial Harm: Evaluating LLM Agent Safety in Executable Economic Worlds
papers.abstract: As LLM agents become increasingly capable of making consequential economic decisions, their safety under economic pressures remains poorly understood. We introduce EconSafeBench, the first benchmark for systematically evaluating the safety of LLM agents in executable economic environments. EconSafeBench contains 828 cases across five economic scenarios and four categories of safety violations. A key design is the matched evaluation of three sources of safety pressure, including explicit user requests, pressure from other actors, and pressure arising from the agent's own pursuit of a performance objective. We further evaluate safety at both static and dynamic scales through 30-period interactions with persistent memory and matched controls. Across eight LLMs, all evaluated models exhibit safety violations on the static benchmark, with overall violation rates ranging from 8.5% to 40.6%. We further find that violations can occur even without an explicit unsafe request, and that initially compliant agents may begin to violate as performance pressure increases over time. These findings highlight the need for stronger safety alignment and rigorous evaluation before LLM agents are deployed in high-stakes economic environments.
papers.summary: As LLM agents become increasingly capable of making consequential economic decisions, their safety under economic pressures remains poorly understood.

sections.title: cs.LG · Machine Learning
sections.name: Machine Learning
sections.focus: energy-efficient and sustainable machine learning: lower compute, carbon and cost
sections.lede: Recent research addresses energy efficiency across machine learning and embedded systems by introducing novel hardware-software co-designs, specialized accelerators, and generative frameworks. These studies demonstrate significant performance speedups and energy reductions, contributing to more sustainable computational and urban infrastructures.

papers.title: ERGo: Energy-Efficient Hybrid Graph Neural Network Training on Processing-In-Memory Architectures
papers.abstract: Processing-in-memory (PIM) has been proposed as an alternative computing paradigm for training Deep Neural Networks, including Graph Neural Networks (GNNs). Despite these advancements, training GNN workloads on PIM devices necessitates off-chip memory access. This off-chip access is expensive in terms of performance and energy, thereby impacting the overall energy efficiency of the training process on PIM platforms. In this paper, we propose a novel hybrid training framework called ERGo that automatically switches from a full-parameter phase to a parameter-efficient phase during the training process with negligible loss in predictive accuracy. The parameter-efficient phase employs low-rank representations of GNN weights, effectively reducing the number of trainable parameters. This helps in reducing the off-chip access during the end-to-end training process on PIM architectures, leading to notable improvements in both performance and energy efficiency. ERGo outperforms the conventional full-parameter GNN training on a PIM-based platform by up to 3.15x in speedup and enhances energy efficiency by 10.5x. Furthermore, ERGo offers additional advantages when utilized on heterogeneous architectures incorporating non-volatile memory (NVM) and static random-access memory (SRAM). Training on the heterogeneous NVM-SRAM architecture typically utilizes NVM for the forward-pass and SRAM for the backward-pass. However, NVM cells suffer from low device endurance and repeated write operations due to weight updates can lead to poor lifetime. ERGo improves the lifetime of NVM devices by freezing the weights and preventing weight updates in the parameter-efficient phase. Experimental results demonstrate that ERGo improves the lifetime of heterogeneous NVM-SRAM architecture by up to 33x in comparison to full-parameter implementation.
papers.summary: The authors propose ERGo, a hybrid training framework for processing-in-memory architectures that automatically switches to a parameter-efficient phase using low-rank representations, achieving up to a 3.15x speedup and a 10.5x improvement in energy efficiency.

papers.title: Matching Architecture to Workload: Comparing RISC-V Parallel Accelerators for Energy-Efficient Embedded Computing
papers.abstract: Embedded computing demands high performance and energy efficiency across workloads with widely different computational characteristics. Choosing the most suitable execution model therefore requires a quantitative understanding of how each model maps to different workload classes. In this paper, we compare three execution models for energy-efficient embedded computing: scalar multicore, stream ing multicore, and vector processing. We use three open-source RISC-V accelerators as representative implementations: the PULP Cluster, the Snitch Cluster, and Spatz, respectively. Their open-source hardware and software stacks enable a controlled comparison based on implementations in the same 12 nm technology and a common benchmark suite. Our results reveal that no single execution model performs best across all workload classes. Spatz delivers the greatest benefits for regular and highly vectorizable compute-intensive applications, achieving up to 4.29x higher performance and 5.17x greater energy efficiency than the other architectures. However, its effectiveness strongly depends on the availability of data-level parallelism and regular computation and memory-access patterns, making it the most sensitive to workload characteristics. The Snitch Cluster performs particularly well on applications with limited parallelism and streamable memory-access patterns, providing up to 5.53x higher performance and 1.45x greater energy efficiency. Conversely, the PULP Cluster is most effective on irregular and control-dominated applications, achieving improvements of up to 5.66x in performance and 2.80x in energy efficiency. Compared with Spatz, however, the greater flexibility offered by PULP and Snitch comes at a non-negligible cost in terms of both area and power.
papers.summary: The authors compare three open-source RISC-V execution models—scalar, streaming, and vector processing—using a 12 nm technology implementation, finding that performance and energy efficiency vary significantly depending on workload characteristics.

papers.title: Splice-Core: Low-Order-Bit-Splicing GEMM for Highly Energy-Efficient AI Inference Accelerators
papers.abstract: Splice-Core is a temporal-unary/binary (tub) hybrid general matrix multiplication (GEMM) unit that minimizes low-order accumulation latency, while retaining value-dependent execution for high-order activation bits. We present two novel processing element (PE) variants: (i) Splice-BP utilizing bit planes, and (ii) Splice-LUT, which selects a shared weight multiple in a single cycle. Compared to a binary systolic array, Splice-BP/Splice-LUT achieve 77.4%/76.4% geometric-mean tile energy reductions, respectively, across 26 INT4 convolutional neural network (CNN) and large language model (LLM) workloads in 45nm. Splice-LUT further increases geometric-mean tile throughput by 44.4% and reduces geometric-mean energy-delay product (EDP) by 6.13x across the 26 configurations. Across the evaluated W8A8 convolution and expert-projection workloads, Splice-BP and Splice-LUT reduce tile energy by 77.3-88.1%. Post-place-and-route INT4 yields 14%/9% smaller area for Splice-BP/Splice-LUT, compared to the systolic array.
papers.summary: The authors introduce Splice-Core, a temporal-unary/binary hybrid GEMM unit that reduces tile energy by 77.4% and 76.4% in Splice-BP and Splice-LUT variants respectively, while achieving substantial improvements in throughput and energy-delay product across evaluated configurations.

papers.title: DySENSE: Dynamic Spatiotemporal ENergy Synthesis and Emulation with Satellite Imagery
papers.abstract: Cities account for over two-thirds of the world's energy and more than 70% of global carbon dioxide emissions. City energy is essential for achieving the 2050 net-zero target and the UN's Sustainable Development Goals 7 and 11. Although existing studies have made progress, they are limited by data and methodological gaps. Existing studies are largely predictive for existing cities rather than generative for future cities; fine-grained, aligned monthly dynamic energy data are scarce; and existing GenAI models struggle to generate dynamic urban functional monthly energy. We present DySENSE, a joint multimodal GenAI framework that synthesizes static urban satellite imagery together with spatially aligned, dynamic monthly building energy consumption maps. We decouple long-term static urban morphology from short-term dynamic energy consumption. By conditioning on static urban land use, DySENSE can generate realistic, diverse and new static urban imagery with aligned energy maps. By conditioning on dynamic monthly and climate prompts, DySENSE can jointly generate dynamic, monthly energy consumption maps while keeping the urban morphology static. Experiments across four cities (New York, Washington, Norfolk, Busan) demonstrated that DySENSE can generate annotated high-fidelity synthetic energy data using less than 25% labelled data, boosting downstream prediction performance by 8% mIoU, and achieving strong energy dynamic consistency. Compared to existing methods, DySENSE significantly improved prediction performance (8.7% accuracy) and reduced prediction error (9%-18% CVRMSE, ASHRAE). DySENSE offers an effective foundation for energy-efficient cities, peak-load analysis, building performance simulation and dynamic demand response for city, energy, and building science. The data and code: https://huggingface.co/datasets/skl24/MUSE2 and https://github.com/kailaisun/DySENSE
papers.summary: The authors introduce DySENSE, a joint multimodal generative AI framework that decouples long-term static urban morphology from short-term dynamic energy consumption to synthesize high-fidelity synthetic energy data using less than 25% labelled data.

papers.title: How to Effectively Manage the Energy in Residential Systems: Development and Comparison of Methods
papers.abstract: The transition from fossil fuels presents significant challenges in energy management. To ensure a sustainable energy future, it is crucial to reduce energy consumption when possible and to synchronize electricity consumption and storage with the production from sources with low greenhouse gas emissions. This thesis explores a variety of energy management methods used to manage batteries, heat pumps, and other energy-related systems. The thesis presents three simulation cases alongside one real-world experiment to compare energy management done through simple rules, optimization, and machine learning methods. Furthermore, this thesis introduces TreeC, a novel machine learning-based method that learns understandable yet efficient energy management strategies, applicable to many cases. The three key contributions of this thesis can be summarized as follows: 1) The developed TreeC method demonstrates competitive performance compared to a variety of energy management approaches, such as model predictive control and reinforcement learning, across a diverse set of energy management problems. The understandability of TreeC's energy management strategies greatly improves the transparency and trustworthiness of machine learning-based energy management. 2) The real-world experiment highlights the need to validate energy management methods on actual hardware and not solely on simulations. Both TreeC and model predictive control performed worse than in simulations, due to, respectively, insufficiently representative training data and the real-time input data not being reliable enough. 3) Energy management algorithms reduce costs in electrified Belgian dwellings, particularly in poorly insulated dwellings, electric vehicle chargers, and photovoltaic installations. However, on average, these cost savings do not yet outweigh the current costs and effort required to implement such algorithms.
papers.summary: The authors explore various residential energy management methods and introduce TreeC, a machine learning-based approach that delivers competitive and transparent performance across diverse energy management problems compared to model predictive control and reinforcement learning.

sections.title: eess.SY · Systems and Control
sections.name: Systems and Control
sections.focus: battery management systems: state-of-charge and state-of-health estimation, degradation modelling and remaining useful life prediction
sections.lede: Recent research in battery management systems and energy storage highlights advances in state-of-health estimation and reinforcement learning controllers. Concurrently, new studies introduce improved cryogenic atom probe tomography workflows, LLM-assisted optimization techniques, and laser processing applications.

papers.title: MARS: Feature-guided physics-informed deep learning for real-time battery health and lifetime prediction
papers.abstract: Accurate and robust estimation of battery state-of-health (SOH) and remaining useful life (RUL) is essential for safe and cost-effective operation of electrified transportation systems, yet it remains challenging under operating variability, non-stationary aging, and non-Gaussian measurement disturbances. This paper proposes Multi-scale Adaptive Robust State Estimation (MARS), a multi-scale adaptive robust state-estimation framework that couples a dual-branch temporal encoder with an equivalent-circuit-model-constrained differentiable generalized-correntropy adaptive Kalman filter. The encoder disentangles fast intra-cycle voltage-current-temperature dynamics from slow inter-cycle degradation, and the fused degradation context adaptively parameterizes the cycle-level process covariance, measurement covariance, and correntropy bandwidth. Through the unrolled robust filtering recursion, MARS performs physics-consistent state propagation and generalized-correntropy-based innovation correction, while uncertainty decomposition and Monte Carlo dropout provide calibrated prediction intervals for SOH estimation and conditional RUL prediction. Experiments on the NASA and CALCE benchmarks demonstrate improved SOH accuracy, achieving mean absolute error/root mean square error values of 0.72%/0.92% and 0.63%/0.80%, respectively, together with competitive conditional RUL performance against representative data-driven and hybrid baselines. The resulting conditional-RUL prediction intervals achieve coverage probabilities of 100.00% and 99.24% on NASA and CALCE, respectively. Ablation, disturbance-sensitivity, near-end-of-life, and runtime analyses further verify the contribution of each module and the practical inference cost for online battery management.
papers.summary: Researchers propose a multi-scale adaptive robust state-estimation framework called MARS that couples a dual-branch temporal encoder with a differentiable generalized-correntropy adaptive Kalman filter, achieving mean absolute error values of 0.72% on NASA and 0.63% on CALCE benchmarks for state-of-health estimation.

papers.title: Accessing Electrode Edges: Upright Mounting for Site-Specific Cryogenic Atom Probe Tomography of Lithium-Ion Batteries
papers.abstract: Cryogenic atom probe tomography (cryo-APT) is increasingly being used to map the three-dimensional distribution of highly reactive species in heterogeneous materials, including those found in battery systems. However, site-specific preparation of localised features and liquid-solid interfaces remains challenging, particularly when regions of interest (ROIs) are concentrated along electrode edges that are difficult to access using conventional mounting geometries. Here, we present a cryo-APT workflow incorporating an upright-mounting procedure that enables targeted specimen preparation of localised regions using plasma focused ion beam (PFIB) microscopy and milling under cryogenic conditions. We first demonstrate the approach using an electrolyte-wetted graphite electrode, successfully preparing and analysing a specimen containing both an edge-localised electrolyte deposit and the underlying graphite and Cu current collector. We then apply the workflow to a cycled graphite electrode, targeting Li dendrites concentrated around the electrode perimeter and successfully preparing and analysing the targeted Li-rich region. Beyond battery systems, this approach offers potential for site-specific cryo-APT of edge-localised features across a broader range of material systems, where conventional specimen preparation geometries may limit access to ROIs.
papers.summary: Cryogenic atom probe tomography (cryo-APT) is increasingly being used to map the three-dimensional distribution of highly reactive species in heterogeneous materials, including those found in battery systems.

papers.title: Battery Energy Storage Sizing in PV Ramp-Rate Smoothing using Constraint-Aware Reinforcement Learning-Based Controller
papers.abstract: This paper presents a constraint-aware reinforcement learning (CARL) controller for battery energy storage system (BESS) sizing and photovoltaic (PV) ramp-rate smoothing. Rapid PV power fluctuations caused by cloud transitions can introduce operational and stability challenges in power systems. To mitigate these impacts, grid codes impose ramp-rate limits (RRL) on PV power injected to the grid. BESSs can support such grid codes by absorbing or supplying power during rapid variations. However, the extent to which BESSs can reduce PV-induced variability depends on (i) the BESS power and energy capacities; and (ii) the adopted controller. Thus, BESS sizing and controller design are coupled. Conventional moving-average control can increase battery usage due to filter-induced lag, while ramp-rate control is reactive and does not account for the long-term impact of actions on battery state of charge and future ramp events. Optimization-based methods can reduce BESS requirements by anticipating future PV variations, but their performance depends on accurate PV forecasts. To address these limitations, the CARL controller learns a causal state-feedback policy from historical PV data without requiring forecasts during deployment. Ramp-rate, converter-power, and state-of-charge constraints are incorporated into a causal feasibility interval that guarantees feasible actions by definition. A full-horizon input-convex neural network (ICNN)-based optimization is developed as a noncausal benchmark for the minimum achievable BESS requirements. Evaluation using three real-world PV datasets shows that, at a 10\%/min ramp-rate limit, CARL reduces peak BESS power by 8.7--10.4\% and energy capacity by 47.5--62.6\% relative to conventional ramp-rate control while maintaining the grid-codes compliance.
papers.summary: The authors present a constraint-aware reinforcement learning controller for battery energy storage sizing and photovoltaic ramp-rate smoothing that learns a causal state-feedback policy from historical data without requiring deployment-time forecasts.

papers.title: LLM-Assisted Multi-Fidelity Bayesian Optimization: Fusing Expert Knowledge with Numerical Data
papers.abstract: Multi-fidelity Bayesian optimization (MFBO) reduces engineering design cost by combining inexpensive low-fidelity (LF) models with a few accurate high-fidelity (HF) evaluations and sequentially selecting designs to evaluate. However, when HF data are scarce, the LF-HF discrepancy is difficult to learn from numerical data alone, especially when physics omitted in the LF model makes it design-dependent. Yet even without sufficient data, domain experts often know which physics the LF model omits and under which conditions its effect grows. Existing multi-fidelity (MF) models cannot use such qualitative knowledge directly, but large language models (LLMs) can interpret it and compare designs accordingly. The proposed LLM-Assisted MFBO adds a knowledge basis to the conventional MF model: from an expert description of the omitted physics, an LLM judges which of two designs requires the larger signed residual correction, and a pairwise Gaussian process converts these judgments into the basis. HF data calibrate its contribution and sign, so the knowledge is not trusted blindly. On a lithium-ion battery design problem, the proposed method reduced the regret area under the curve of conventional MFBO by 61%. Knowledge quality, rather than the choice of LLM, determined whether the search was accelerated, as shown by a controlled study that varied the two independently. A knowledge-level ablation further quantified the contribution of each knowledge statement. These results show that LLM-interpreted expert knowledge can complement numerical data as an information source in MFBO.
papers.summary: Multi-fidelity Bayesian optimization (MFBO) reduces engineering design cost by combining inexpensive low-fidelity (LF) models with a few accurate high-fidelity (HF) evaluations and sequentially selecting designs to evaluate.

papers.title: Laser Processing for Energy Applications
papers.abstract: Laser processing has emerged as a transformative technology in the energy sector, enabling precise, efficient, and scalable solutions for energy generation, storage, and sustainability. This chapter explores the diverse applications of laser technology in energy applications. It begins with an overview of laser-driven inertial confinement fusion for energy production, highlighting key experimental facilities and crucial laser parameters. The role of lasers in solar energy harvesting is examined, including photovoltaic cell optimization, concentrated solar power, and laser-assisted recycling of solar modules. The chapter further reviews recent developments into laser-based techniques for enhancing electrochemical performance through surface texturing at various scales. Advancements in lithium-ion battery technology are also discussed, focusing on next-generation materials, battery manufacturing processes, and the impact of laser techniques on performance, safety, and scalability. The chapter concludes with insights into future prospects for laser applications in sustainable energy solutions.
papers.summary: Laser processing has emerged as a transformative technology in the energy sector, enabling precise, efficient, and scalable solutions for energy generation, storage, and sustainability.
